key_insight: The Personal Imitation Game shifts the question from “Can AI pass as human?” to “Can AI pass as a specific person?” A study with 30 participants establishes a human baseline and identifies writing style, personality, and biographical facts as key identity signals.
problem_solved: Generic human-like conversation does not show whether an AI can convincingly replicate an individual. This work proposes a framework for evaluating person-specific conversational imitation.
method: Introduce a Personal Imitation Game focused on recognizing a specific individual's conversational identity.
Test with 30 participants to establish a human baseline.
Examine the identity cues interrogators use: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts.
impact: The framework gives AI/ML practitioners a way to evaluate personalized conversational systems beyond generic fluency. It also highlights identity cues relevant to assessing impersonation risks; the supplied abstract is truncated and does not provide results for the proposed LLM-based system.
visual_elements: Side-by-side comparison: classic Turing Test (“Human or machine?”) versus Personal Imitation Game (“Which person?”).
Conversation diagram connecting an interrogator, a target individual, and an AI imitator.
Three identity-signal icons: writing style, personality, and biography.
A 30-person participant graphic representing the human-baseline study.
paper_title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
paper_authors: Muhammad Rizky Wellyanto, Hajara-Yasmin Isa, Kexin Xue, Vishal Ravichandran, Wenpeng Lu
